plain_title: LSD, mushrooms, ketamine, PCP: when use becomes a problem
one_liner: Problems from hallucinogens such as LSD, psilocybin, MDMA-like drugs, ketamine, or PCP, including use disorders and lasting perception changes.
in_simple_words: Hallucinogens change perception, thought, and mood. Most people who use them don't develop a use disorder; dependence is uncommon with classic psychedelics and more common with PCP and ketamine. Problems include frightening or dangerous intoxication, triggering psychosis in vulnerable people, and hallucinogen persisting perception disorder (HPPD), where visual disturbances continue long after use. Ketamine can also damage the bladder. This card is about harm, not about the controlled clinical trials of psychedelic therapies.
what_it_can_feel_like: The trip itself was fine. The visual snow six months later wasn't.
Ketamine went from weekends to every day without me noticing the line.
I didn't think you could get hooked on it. The bladder pain is what finally got me into treatment.
common_signs: Using more or more often than intended, especially with ketamine or PCP
Risky behaviour or injuries during intoxication
Lasting visual disturbances (trails, halos, 'visual snow') after use has stopped
Paranoia, panic, or psychotic symptoms during or after use
With ketamine: bladder pain, urinary problems, memory problems

myths_vs_facts.myth: Psychedelics can't be addictive, so there's no risk.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Classic psychedelics rarely cause dependence, but ketamine and PCP can, and all of them can trigger dangerous reactions or psychosis in some people.

myths_vs_facts.myth: A bad trip means permanent damage.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Most bad trips pass within hours with a calm setting. Lasting problems are uncommon, and HPPD is treatable.

myths_vs_facts.myth: If researchers are studying psychedelics for depression, self-medicating is fine.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Clinical trials use screened participants, known doses, and trained support. None of that is true of unsupervised use.

how_common.plain: Hallucinogen use disorder is uncommon compared with other substance use disorders. HPPD is rare, affecting a small minority of people who have used hallucinogens.
how_common.figure: DSM-5-TR text: 12-month prevalence of other hallucinogen use disorder about 0.1% of adults; HPPD estimated at around 4% of hallucinogen users in older studies
how_common.note: Figures from the DSM-5-TR text; need primary sources.

what_helps.plain_summary: Treatment follows the general approach for substance use disorders: CBT, motivational interviewing, and peer support, with medical care for ketamine-related bladder damage. HPPD is treated with reassurance, avoiding further hallucinogen and cannabis use, and sometimes medication, prescribed and monitored by a doctor. Psychotic symptoms that persist need psychiatric assessment. Frightening intoxication is managed with a calm, safe setting and, if needed, medical care.
evidence_based_options: CBT and motivational interviewing for ketamine or PCP use disorder
Medical assessment and treatment for ketamine bladder damage
Assessment and care for persisting psychotic symptoms
Reassurance, abstinence, and sometimes medication for HPPD, prescribed and monitored by a doctor
self_help_that_supports_care: Stopping all hallucinogens and cannabis if HPPD symptoms appear
Never using alone or in an unsafe place
Telling a doctor about bladder symptoms early
Peer support with others who've stopped

when_to_reach_out: If ketamine or PCP use is becoming hard to control, if you have visual disturbances that won't go away, or if paranoia or hearing voices persist after use, talk to a doctor or a drug helpline. Get emergency help for severe agitation, high temperature, or unresponsiveness.
is_not: Having used a hallucinogen, even having had a bad trip, isn't a disorder. Prescribed ketamine or esketamine for depression under medical supervision is a treatment, not a use disorder.
hope_note: Lasting harm from hallucinogens is uncommon, and where it occurs, people recover with abstinence and support.

content_notes: No dosing, sourcing, or 'how to use' detail. Harm-reduction pointers only to official organizations.
Crisis strip with substance helplines required.

open_questions: Find primary prevalence sources for hallucinogen use disorder and HPPD.

in_young_people: Ketamine use has grown among young people in several countries, with bladder damage appearing in people in their early twenties. Honest information works better than scare tactics.
across_cultures: Some hallucinogens have long-standing ceremonial use in Indigenous cultures, which the DSM distinguishes from a disorder. Patterns of problem use differ by country: ketamine in parts of Asia and the UK, PCP in some US cities.

sub_sections.title: Phencyclidine (PCP) use disorder and intoxication
sub_sections.text: PCP can cause dangerous agitation, violence, and injuries during intoxication, and dependence is more common than with classic psychedelics.

sub_sections.title: Hallucinogen persisting perception disorder
sub_sections.text: Re-experiencing visual disturbances, like trails, halos, or 'visual snow', long after use has stopped, causing distress. Uncommon and treatable.
